cards.back: Emits ${}_{2}^{4}\text{He}$; same as a helium nucleus; lowest penetrating power.
Emits ${}_{-1}^{0}e$; same as an electron; medium penetrating power.
Emits ${}_{0}^{0}\gamma$; no mass + no charge; most damaging / highest penetrating power.
Alpha ($\alpha$) < Beta ($\beta$) < Gamma ($\gamma$).
Nuclear decay reactions involve changes in an atom’s nucleus that produce radiation (alpha, beta, gamma).

cards.back: Metals are mostly on the left of the periodic table; nonmetals are on the right.
Make up the majority of the periodic table and are generally good conductors, malleable, ductile, and shiny.
Brittle, poor conductors, and dull.
They are along the diagonal stair-step line on the periodic table (Boron (B), Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb), Tellurium (Te)).
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.
Alkali Metals (most reactive metals).
Alkaline Earth Metals (highly reactive, shiny, and silvery-white mostly).
Halogens (most reactive nonmetals).
Noble Gases (non-reactive / stable, full valence shell).
Elements in the same period have the same number of energy levels.

cards.front: Atomic radius trend on periodic table
cards.back:
Increases $\downarrow$ down a group.
Decreases $\rightarrow$ across a period.

cards.front: Electronegativity/ionization energy trend across a period
cards.back:
Increases $\rightarrow$ across a period.
Decreases $\downarrow$ down a group.
Loses electrons $\rightarrow$ SMALLER.
Gains electrons $\rightarrow$ BIGGER.
Count protons ($p^+$): more $p^+$ $\rightarrow$ stronger nuclear pull $\rightarrow$ SMALLER; less $p^+$ $\rightarrow$ weaker nuclear pull $\rightarrow$ BIGGER.

cards.front: Which of $\text{F, Br, Cl}$ has the largest atomic radius?
cards.back: $\text{Br}$ is largest.

cards.front: Rank in decreasing atomic radius ($\text{F, Br, Cl}$)
cards.back: $\text{Br} > \text{Cl} > \text{F}$.
$\text{S}^{2-}$ is bigger, because both have 18 electrons, but $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has 20 protons while $\text{S}^{2-}$ has 16 protons; more nuclear pull in $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ makes it smaller.
When the charges get larger between two particles, attraction increases. When the distance between the charges gets larger, attraction decreases.
A physical process in which the heavy nucleus of an atom splits into two or more smaller nuclei, releasing a massive amount of energy.
A nuclear process that involves 2 small nuclei combining to form 1 bigger nucleus releasing a very large amount of energy, however not more than fission.
